title: Invoice Submission: Finance Bottleneck or Self-Service?
summary: Should every employee submit invoices or should finance key them all? Compare the two invoice submission models on speed, control, quality and licence cost.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Every growing company eventually has to decide whether invoices flow through a small finance team that keys everything, or whether the people who buy things submit their own invoices. Centralised submission protects data quality but creates a queue. Self-service submission removes the queue but risks unreadable documents, wrong coding and invoices routed to the wrong approver, and it can multiply software seats. The model that works for most multi-entity businesses is hybrid: submitters provide only a readable document and its purpose, validation happens at upload, AI suggests coding, finance triages before approval, and licensing uses lightweight roles or seatless channels for occasional submitters.


## Introduction


There is a moment in most finance teams’ growth when the invoice inbox stops being manageable. Invoices arrive from suppliers, from staff who bought something on the business’s behalf, from site managers, from department heads, and they all converge on two or three people in finance.


Finance leaders we speak with frame the decision clearly. They want people across the group to submit invoices independently rather than everything going through one bottleneck in finance. In the same breath they raise two concerns: frontline staff cannot be expected to validate accounting codes, and if every submitter becomes a software user, the licence cost changes significantly. One multi-entity team we spoke with weighed a model with around 200 submitters against a finance-only model with roughly ten users.


This guide sets out the two models, what each one costs and protects, and how to design a submission step that gets the speed of self-service without losing control.


## What Is Invoice Submission?


**Invoice submission is the step where a supplier invoice enters the accounts payable process.** It covers every channel by which a document reaches AP: a supplier emailing an AP inbox, an employee uploading a photo, a vendor using a portal, or finance keying a paper invoice. It determines who is responsible for getting the document, and the context around it, into the system.


Submission is easy to overlook because it feels administrative. In practice it decides how quickly invoices are captured, how many are lost, how clean the data is when it arrives and how much finance spends correcting it. It sits upstream of everything in[AI-powered invoice capture](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable/bills-and-ocr-ai-powered-invoice-capture) , approval and payment.


## The Two Invoice Submission Models


### Centralised submission


Employees and suppliers send invoices to finance, usually by email. Finance enters or captures every invoice, codes it and sends it for approval. Only finance users need access to the AP system.


### Self-service submission


The employee who made the purchase submits the invoice directly into the AP system, typically from mobile. Finance reviews submissions, confirms coding and lets them proceed to approval. Every submitter needs some form of access.


Dimension Centralised (finance keys everything) Self-service (buyers submit)


Purchase-to-capture time Slow, queues behind finance capacity Fast, captured when the buyer receives it


Lost or forgotten invoices Common, invoices sit in personal inboxes Rare, if submission is easy


Data quality at entry High, entered by trained staff Variable, depends on design


Context about the purchase Often missing, finance has to ask Captured from the person who knows


Finance workload High and linear with volume Lower, shifts to review


Number of system users Small Large


Licence cost Lower Higher, unless designed carefully


Accountability Finance owns everything Buyer owns submission, finance owns accuracy


Neither model is wrong. They optimise for different things, and the right answer depends on volume, the number of people who buy and how much capacity finance has. For Singapore SMEs weighing this as part of a wider digitalisation plan,[IMDA](https://www.imda.gov.sg/) publishes guidance on adopting digital solutions in stages rather than all at once.


## Why Centralised Submission Becomes a Bottleneck


Centralised submission works well at low volume. It degrades as the business grows, for three reasons.


**Queues grow linearly.** Every additional invoice adds the same amount of finance work. There is no economy of scale in keying.


**Context is missing.** Finance receives an invoice for a purchase it did not make and has to ask the buyer what it was for, which cost centre it belongs to and whether the goods arrived. Each question is an email and a wait.


**Invoices go missing upstream.** The invoice never reaches finance because it sits in a site manager’s bag, inbox or phone gallery. It surfaces when the supplier chases, often past due. Our analysis of[manual routing as an approval bottleneck](https://peakflo.co/blog/approval-workflow-bottlenecks-manual-routing) shows how the same queueing effect compounds at the approval stage.


Professional bodies such as the[Association for Financial Professionals](https://www.afponline.org/) consistently find that late-arriving and exception invoices, rather than routine processing, drive much of AP cost and supplier friction.


## Why Self-Service Submission Goes Wrong Without Design


Opening submission to everyone removes the queue but introduces four new risks.


### Unreadable documents


Frontline staff photograph invoices on the spot, often at an angle, in poor light or with part of the document cut off. If the system accepts anything, finance discovers the problem later and has to chase. The fix is validation at upload, which we cover in detail in[ending the phone photo chase loop](https://peakflo.co/blog/phone-photo-invoice-capture-submitter-chase-loop) .


### Coding by people who do not know the chart of accounts


Asking a store manager or driver to choose a GL account produces guesses. Training rarely fixes it. The better answer is to remove the field from their screen, which is the argument made in[stop asking frontline staff to code GL](https://peakflo.co/blog/restrict-gl-coding-field-permissions-submitters) .


### Routing to the wrong approver


When approval routing depends on coding, such as by vendor category, budget category or cost centre, a wrongly coded invoice goes to the wrong approver. That approver either rejects it or, worse, approves something outside their budget. Finance then has to reverse the flow. Many teams therefore decide that non-finance submitters should not be able to send invoices for approval themselves, which is consistent with the[COSO framework](https://www.coso.org/) principle that a review should sit between initiating a transaction and authorising it.


### Licence cost


Many AP platforms price partly per user. Moving from ten finance users to a couple of hundred submitters can change the commercial picture significantly, which is why the submission model and the licensing model have to be designed together.


Self-service risk Root cause Design control


Unreadable documents No validation at upload Readability and field checks with instant feedback


Wrong GL coding Submitters see and choose coding fields Hide coding from submitters, AI suggests, finance confirms


Wrong approver Routing depends on unverified coding Finance triage step before approval


Duplicate submissions Same invoice sent by buyer and supplier Duplicate detection at capture


Rising licence cost Every submitter is a full user Lightweight roles or seatless channels


## The Hybrid Model That Works for Most Growing Businesses


The choice is rarely binary. Most multi-entity finance teams end up with a hybrid that routes each invoice source through the channel that suits it.


Invoice source Recommended channel Needs a user seat? Who reviews


Regular suppliers with high volume Supplier emails AP inbox or uses vendor portal No Finance


Employees making occasional purchases Mobile upload with a lightweight submitter role Usually a light role Finance, then approver


Field and site staff with paper invoices Photo upload or messaging channel Often no Finance


Department heads with recurring vendors Self-service with coding hidden Yes Finance, then approver


Paper invoices posted to the office Finance scans and captures No Finance


Supplier-facing channels such as a[vendor portal](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable/vendor-portal) shift submission to the party that issues the invoice, which removes the employee from the loop entirely for routine suppliers.


## How to Choose an Invoice Submission Model: Six Steps


**Step 1: Map where invoices originate.** List every channel invoices arrive through and who physically receives them. Include the field staff, store managers and department heads who are never in the finance org chart but hold invoices every week.


**Step 2: Measure the current bottleneck.** Track how long invoices wait between receipt by the buyer and capture by finance, and count how many surface only when a supplier chases. These two numbers usually make the case for change on their own.


**Step 3: Decide what submitters must provide.** Ask submitters only for what they uniquely know: a readable document, the purpose of the purchase and, where relevant, confirmation that goods or services were received. Everything else is extracted or suggested.


**Step 4: Add validation at the point of upload.** Check readability, required fields and duplicates while the submitter is still holding the document. Tell them immediately if it cannot be used.


**Step 5: Insert a finance triage step before approval.** Let finance confirm the entity, coding and approver before the invoice routes. This is fast when AI has already suggested the coding, and it stops reverse flows.


**Step 6: Choose the licensing shape.** Compare full users, lightweight submitter roles and seatless channels such as email intake, messaging and vendor portals. Model both the finance-only and the all-submitter scenarios before committing.


## What Should Submitters See?


The single most effective design decision in self-service submission is limiting the submitter screen to what the submitter can actually answer.


Field Shown to submitter? Source


Invoice image or file Yes Submitter


Purpose of purchase Yes Submitter


Goods or service received Yes, where relevant Submitter


Vendor, date, amount, tax Shown read-only for confirmation AI extraction


Entity Pre-filled from submitter profile System


GL account and cost centre No AI suggestion confirmed by finance


Approver No Routing rules after finance triage


Role-based access of this kind is a basic access control principle.[ISACA](https://www.isaca.org/) guidance on application controls stresses giving each role access only to the fields it needs, both for data quality and for control.


## How Peakflo Supports Both Submission Models


Peakflo is designed so finance teams can pick the model per entity, per supplier type and per user group.


- **Multiple intake channels.** Invoices arrive by email inbox, web or mobile upload, the vendor portal and a[WhatsApp vendor portal](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable/whatsapp-vendor-portal) for suppliers who prefer messaging.
- **Image and handwriting capture.** AI capture reads photographed and handwritten invoices and automatically emails the submitter when a document cannot be read.
- **Role-based field permissions.** The chart of accounts field can be greyed out or hidden for submitters, while AI suggests coding for finance to confirm.
- **Finance triage before approval.** Submitters can be prevented from sending for approval, so finance confirms coding before routing by amount, vendor category or budget category.
- **Mobile throughout.** Submission and approval both work on mobile, which matters for field and site teams, as discussed in[email and mobile approval adoption](https://peakflo.co/blog/email-mobile-expense-approval-adoption) .


## What Metrics Show the Submission Model Is Working?


Metric What it reveals Healthy direction


Purchase-to-capture time Whether invoices enter the system promptly Falling to days, not weeks


Submissions failing validation Quality of inbound documents Falling, with instant resubmission


Invoices corrected by finance before approval How much triage effort remains Falling as AI coding learns


Invoices first seen when a supplier chases Invoices lost upstream Near zero


Cost per active submitter Whether licensing matches usage Stable or falling


[IFAC](https://www.ifac.org/) guidance on finance function effectiveness recommends measuring process quality at each hand-off rather than only end-to-end cycle time. Submission is the first hand-off, so it deserves its own metrics.


## Our Verdict: Which Invoice Submission Model Should You Choose?


After working through this decision with multi-entity finance teams, our view is that pure centralised submission rarely survives growth, and pure self-service rarely survives first contact with frontline staff. The answer is a designed hybrid.


### Move towards self-service submission if


- Invoices regularly surface only when suppliers chase
- Many people across sites or entities make purchases
- Finance spends significant time asking buyers what purchases were for
- You can hide coding from submitters and validate at upload
- Lightweight roles or seatless channels keep licence cost reasonable


### Keep submission centralised for now if


- Invoice volume is low and comes mainly from a few regular suppliers
- Few employees make purchases
- Finance has spare capacity and invoices are captured promptly


**Our Recommendation** : Route routine suppliers through an inbox or vendor portal, give occasional buyers a mobile submission path that asks only for a readable document and its purpose, keep coding with AI and finance, and insert a finance triage step before approval. Model licence cost for both the finance-only and the all-submitter scenarios before rollout, so the submission design and the commercial model match.


## Conclusion


The question is not whether finance should be a bottleneck or whether everyone should submit invoices. It is which invoices should come through which channel, what each submitter should be asked to provide and where finance should check before approval.


Get those three decisions right and you remove the queue without inheriting bad data, keep coding where the expertise is, stop invoices going to the wrong approver and avoid paying for seats that do not need to exist. That combination is what lets AP scale with the business instead of with headcount.

## Frequently Asked Questions


**What is invoice submission in accounts payable?** Invoice submission is the step where a supplier invoice enters the AP process, whether it is forwarded by email, uploaded by an employee, sent through a vendor portal or keyed in by finance. It decides who is responsible for getting the document, and its context, into the system.


**What is the difference between centralised and self-service invoice submission?** In a centralised model, employees hand invoices to finance and a small finance team enters everything. In a self-service model, the employee who made the purchase submits the invoice directly into the AP system, and finance reviews it afterwards.


**Which invoice submission model is faster?** Self-service is usually faster from purchase to capture because the invoice enters the system when the buyer receives it. Centralised submission is slower because invoices queue behind finance capacity, but it can produce cleaner data at the point of entry.


**Does self-service invoice submission mean frontline staff must code invoices?** No. A well designed self-service model asks submitters only for what they uniquely know, such as the purpose of the purchase and a readable document. GL coding is suggested by AI and confirmed by finance, and the coding field can be hidden from submitters entirely.


**Should submitters be allowed to send invoices for approval themselves?** Usually not when submitters are non-finance staff. If coding drives approval routing, an incorrectly coded invoice will go to the wrong approver. A finance review step between submission and approval prevents those reverse flows.


**How does the submission model affect AP software licence cost?** Many AP platforms price partly by user, so letting every buyer submit can multiply seats compared with a finance-only model. Options that reduce cost include lightweight submitter roles, email or messaging intake that needs no seat and vendor portal submission.


**How do you make sure self-submitted invoices are usable?** Validate at upload. Check that the image is readable, required fields can be extracted and the document is not a duplicate, and tell the submitter immediately if it fails, rather than letting finance discover the problem later.


**Can a company use both submission models?** Yes, and most growing businesses should. A hybrid model lets high-volume, routine suppliers submit through a vendor portal or a shared inbox handled by finance, while employees who make occasional purchases submit their own invoices from mobile.


**When does centralised invoice submission still make sense?** When invoice volume is low, most invoices come from a few regular suppliers by email, the finance team has capacity and few employees make purchases. In that situation the cost of extra users may outweigh the speed benefit.


**What metrics show whether the invoice submission model is working?** Track purchase-to-capture time, the share of submissions that fail validation, the share of invoices finance has to correct before approval, invoices discovered only when a supplier chases and the cost per active submitter.
